content: Seventeen studies included a total of 1,276 participants who were either HIV-negative or whose HIV status was unknown. Five studies included 317 participants living with HIV (PLHIV), and four studies included 34 participants under the age of 18. Among the included studies, 14 evaluated the diagnostic performance of the Diaskintest, four assessed Cy-Tb, and three examined C-TST. These findings are detailed in Figures 1–4, as referenced in Web Annex A. The pooled sensitivity of the tests against the microbiological reference standard for tuberculosis (TB) disease was evaluated in six head-to-head studies. The evidence was deemed to be of high certainty and was not downgraded. Studies by Starshinova in 2018 and 2019 evaluated Diaskintest results using a cut-off of at least 5 mm of induration. Other studies were head-to-head comparisons of Cy-Tb, which also used a 5 mm cut-off. For tuberculin skin tests (TST), the cut-off was 5 mm for PLHIV and 15 mm for HIV-negative individuals in four studies. Only studies on Diaskintest and Cy-Tb were included in this analysis. The pooled sensitivity in 17 studies is presented in Figure 8. Sensitivity estimates were lower in studies using Diaskintest with any induration size as a positive result. The reasons for this lower sensitivity are unclear but may reflect differences in study populations or quality. Consequently, the certainty of evidence was downgraded one level for inconsistency and another for imprecision, resulting in very low certainty. Despite the manufacturer's recommendation to use any induration size as a positive result, studies using a 5 mm cut-off for Diaskintest showed sensitivity more aligned with other tests in the same class, which also used a 5 mm cut-off. The risk of bias was considered serious due to the potential for knowledge of reference standards to influence the interpretation of index test results. In most Diaskintest studies, participant selection and reference standard determination were unclear, leading to a downgrade in evidence certainty for risk of bias. Sensitivity ranged from 55% to 100%, with the reasons for this heterogeneity remaining unknown. As a result, the overall certainty of evidence was considered low. Specificity was evaluated in 14 studies involving 3,792 participants, including 1,104 children and adolescents and 587 BCG-vaccinated individuals. Specificity was measured in healthy individuals with negative interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) results. Differences in specificity were calculated as the proportion of negative results between TB antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) and TST or IGRAs in healthy populations. Specificity was high for all three TBSTs in the class, as shown in Figure 5. However, the overall certainty of evidence for specificity was very low due to the inclusion of studies of very low quality. In children and adolescents, specificity was high in two studies involving 176 participants with negative IGRA results. The difference in specificity between TBSTs and TST ranged from –2% to 72%, with the certainty of evidence downgraded for inconsistency. The overall certainty of evidence for specificity differences between TBSTs and TST was low. Agreement between index tests and comparator tests (TST or IGRAs) was assessed in 16 studies involving 3,198 participants, including four studies with 1,307 participants under 18 years of age. Agreement was high (≥90%) for Cy-Tb and Diaskintest (any induration size and 5 mm induration) compared with QuantiFERON-TB Gold (QFT). However, agreement ranged widely (61% to 97%) across various tests and studies, leading to a downgrade in evidence certainty for inconsistency. The overall certainty of evidence for agreement between TBSTs and IGRAs was low. Safety data were systematically reviewed, focusing on local reactions (injection site reactions, ISR) and systemic adverse events associated with TBSTs. Seven studies for Cy-Tb, five for C-TST, and 11 for Diaskintest were identified. Cy-Tb studies were conducted in South Africa and Europe, with 20–40% of participants in South African studies being PLHIV. C-TST studies were conducted in China and included only HIV-negative adults. Diaskintest studies were primarily cross-sectional and conducted in the Russian Federation and Ukraine, involving various populations, including children and adolescents. The pooled risk of any ISR due to Cy-Tb (five studies) and Diaskintest (one study) is presented in Figure 10. The Diaskintest study had a high risk of bias, but the overall certainty of evidence from randomized controlled trials for any ISR was judged as high. For systemic reactions, the overall certainty of evidence was moderate due to small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. Based on the totality of data, the safety profile of novel TBSTs was considered similar to that of TST, with mostly mild ISRs such as itching and pain. However, regulatory safety assessments are needed before implementing TBST products. Cost and cost-effectiveness analyses were conducted through two systematic reviews. The primary review focused on novel TBSTs (Diaskintest, C-TST, and Cy-Tb), while the secondary review examined TST and IGRA tests. Economic evaluations were based on a health provider perspective and related to TB infection diagnostics.
